:::{#thm-moore-penrose-exists}
#### Every matrix has a Moore-Penrose inverse

Every $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$ has a Moore-Penrose inverse (@def-moore-penrose),
written $\matr{A}^+$; it is unique by @thm-moore-penrose-unique.

- If $\matr{A} = \matr{0}_{m \times n}$, then $\matr{A}^+ = \matr{0}_{n \times m}$.
- If $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = r \ge 1$ and $\matr{A} = \matr{C} \matr{R}$
  is a rank factorization (@def-rank-factorization), then

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}^+}_{n \times m}
= \underbrace{\tp{\matr{R}}}_{n \times r}
  \underbrace{(\matr{R} \tp{\matr{R}})^{-1}}_{r \times r}
  \underbrace{(\tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C})^{-1}}_{r \times r}
  \underbrace{\tp{\matr{C}}}_{r \times m}.
$$

:::

::: proof

**The two cases cover every matrix.**
If $\matr{A} \ne \matr{0}_{m \times n}$, it has a nonzero column,
which is linearly independent on its own
($c\,\vecf{v} = \vzero$ with $\vecf{v} \ne \vzero$ forces $c = 0$),
so $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) \ge 1$ (@def-rank).

**The zero matrix.**
With $\matr{A} = \matr{0}_{m \times n}$ and $\matr{G} = \matr{0}_{n \times m}$,
every product in conditions 1 to 4 is a zero matrix,
and a zero matrix equals its own transpose,
so all four conditions hold.

**The two inverses exist.**
Now suppose $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = r \ge 1$.
A rank factorization exists (@thm-rank-factorization).
$\matr{C}$ is $m \times r$ and $\matr{R}$ is $r \times n$.
Both have rank $r$:

$$
\ba
r
&= \operatorname{rank}(\matr{C} \matr{R})
&& \text{(} \matr{A} = \matr{C} \matr{R} \text{)}
\\
&\le \operatorname{rank}(\matr{C})
&& \text{(@thm-rank-product)}
\\
&\le r,
&& \text{(@cor-rank-bound, } \matr{C} \text{ has } r \text{ columns)}
\ea
$$

and, using $\tp{(\matr{C} \matr{R})} = \tp{\matr{R}} \tp{\matr{C}}$ (@thm-transpose-product),

$$
\ba
r
&= \operatorname{rank}\paren{\tp{\matr{R}} \tp{\matr{C}}}
&& \text{(@thm-rank-transpose)}
\\
&\le \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{R}})
&& \text{(@thm-rank-product)}
\\
&\le r.
&& \text{(@cor-rank-bound, } \tp{\matr{R}} \text{ has } r \text{ columns)}
\ea
$$

So $\matr{C}$ and $\tp{\matr{R}}$ have full column rank $r$,
and $\tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C}$ and $\matr{R} \tp{\matr{R}} = \tp{(\tp{\matr{R}})}\,\tp{\matr{R}}$
are invertible (@thm-gram-invertible).
They are symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tp{(\tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C})} &= \tp{\matr{C}}\,\tp{(\tp{\matr{C}})} \\
&= \tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C}
\end{aligned}
$$

(@thm-transpose-product, @def-matrix-transpose), and likewise for $\matr{R} \tp{\matr{R}}$.
Write $\matr{S} \eqdef (\matr{R} \tp{\matr{R}})^{-1}$
and $\matr{T} \eqdef (\tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C})^{-1}$,
both symmetric (@cor-inverse-symmetric),
and $\matr{G} \eqdef \tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}$.

**Two products.**

$$
\ba
\matr{A} \matr{G}
&= \matr{C} \matr{R}\,\tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(substitute } \matr{A} \text{ and } \matr{G} \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{C}\,(\matr{R} \tp{\matr{R}})\,\matr{S}\,\matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{C}\,\matr{I}_r\,\matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{C} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}},
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\matr{G} \matr{A}
&= \tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}\,\matr{C} \matr{R}
&& \text{(substitute } \matr{G} \text{ and } \matr{A} \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S}\,\matr{T}\,(\tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C})\,\matr{R}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S}\,\matr{I}_r\,\matr{R}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{R}.
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\ea
$$

**Conditions 3 and 4.**

$$
\ba
\tp{(\matr{A} \matr{G})}
&= \tp{(\matr{C} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}})}
&& \text{(first product)}
\\
&= \tp{\paren{\matr{C}\,(\matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}})}}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \tp{(\matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}})}\,\tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \tp{(\tp{\matr{C}})}\,\tp{\matr{T}}\,\tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \matr{C}\,\tp{\matr{T}}\,\tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-transpose)}
\\
&= \matr{C} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}},
&& \text{(} \matr{T} \text{ is symmetric)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\tp{(\matr{G} \matr{A})}
&= \tp{(\tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{R})}
&& \text{(second product)}
\\
&= \tp{\paren{\tp{\matr{R}}\,(\matr{S} \matr{R})}}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \tp{(\matr{S} \matr{R})}\,\tp{(\tp{\matr{R}})}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}}\,\tp{\matr{S}}\,\tp{(\tp{\matr{R}})}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}}\,\tp{\matr{S}}\,\matr{R}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-transpose)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{R}.
&& \text{(} \matr{S} \text{ is symmetric)}
\ea
$$

**Condition 1.**

$$
\ba
\matr{A} \matr{G} \matr{A}
&= \matr{C} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}\,\matr{C} \matr{R}
&& \text{(first product)}
\\
&= \matr{C}\,\matr{T}\,(\tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C})\,\matr{R}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{C}\,\matr{I}_r\,\matr{R}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{A}.
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\ea
$$

**Condition 2.**

$$
\ba
\matr{G} \matr{A} \matr{G}
&= \tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{R}\,\tp{\matr{R}} \matr{S} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(second product)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}}\,\matr{S}\,(\matr{R} \tp{\matr{R}})\,\matr{S}\,\matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{R}}\,\matr{I}_r\,\matr{S}\,\matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{G}.
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\ea
$$

:::

:::{#exm-moore-penrose-exists}
#### The Moore-Penrose inverse of a rank-one matrix

For $\matr{A}$ in @exm-column-space, the rank factorization
$\matr{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$,
$\matr{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$
(@exm-rank-factorization) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tp{\matr{C}} \matr{C} &= 1 + 9 \\
&= 10
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{R} \tp{\matr{R}} &= 1 + 4 + 4 \\
&= 9,
\end{aligned}
$$

so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{A}^+
&= \frac{1}{9 \cd 10} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \frac{1}{90} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -6 \\ -2 & -6 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

As a check on condition 1,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{A} \matr{A}^+ &= \matr{C} \matr{T} \tp{\matr{C}} \\
&= \frac{1}{10} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9 \end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
$$

and its first row times $\matr{A}$ is
$\frac{1}{10}\paren{1 \cd (1, -2, -2) + 3 \cd (3, -6, -6)} = (1, -2, -2)$,
the first row of $\matr{A}$; the second row is $3$ times the first,
like the second row of $\matr{A}$.

:::
